articles.title: Who are Yemen's Houthis and what do they want?
articles.summary:
Who are Yemen's Houthis and what do they want?

Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 10/12/2026 - 09:45
Yemen's war has reignited, pulling in Saudi Arabia's allies and threatening one of the world's most important shipping lanes
Supporters of Ansar Allah hold up a portrait of the group's leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, during a protest against the Saudi intervention in Yemen in Sanaa on 18 September 2026 (AFP)
Off

A strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday killed 13 people and wounded 309, in the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in more than a decade. Another strike on the airport on Sunday killed one more person.

The Saudi-led coalition blamed Yemen's Houthis and called the attack a war crime.

In a statement on Sunday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had targeted the airport "in three stages" since Friday evening, closing it completely, and warned that Saudi airports were "unsafe", except those serving Mecca and Medina.

The attack capped a summer of escalation. A UN-backed truce that had largely frozen Yemen's war since 2022 broke down in July after Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport, and the Houthis then declared a maritime blockade on the kingdom.

In September, the Sanaa-based group seized the Red Sea port of Mokha and pushed towards the Bab al-Mandab strait.

Saudi-backed government forces launched a counter-offensive in early October, and the UN special envoy has warned that Yemen has returned to full-scale war.

Heavy clashes are continuing around the strategically important city of Taiz, which sits above the Red Sea coast. The renewed fighting has displaced 130,000 people.

Who are the Houthis?

Officially known as Ansar Allah, or "helpers of God", the movement emerged in Yemen's far north in the 1990s around the cleric Hussein al-Houthi.

It is rooted in Zaydism, a branch of Shia Islam whose followers are a minority in Yemen but concentrated in the northern highlands.

The group fought six rounds of war with the government of former president Ali Abdullah Saleh between 2004 and 2010. Hussein al-Houthi was killed in the first and leadership passed to his brother, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, who still heads the movement.

Houthi fighters captured Sanaa in September 2014, and in March 2015, Saudi Arabia led a military coalition into Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government, which has mostly governed from Riyadh and the southern Yemeni city of Aden.

By the time of the 2022 truce, the Houthis held about 30 percent of Yemen's territory but around 80 percent of its population.

What do they want?

At home, the Houthis have sought greater autonomy for the north and, increasingly, recognition as Yemen's governing authority.

What would Houthi control of Bab al-Mandeb mean for the region?
Read More »

They have demanded an end to what they describe as a Saudi land, air and naval siege of Yemen, a characterisation Riyadh rejects.

In his statement on Sunday, Saree said the group would keep escalating attacks deep inside Saudi Arabia under what he called an equation of "siege for siege, escalation for escalation", until the "aggression" stopped and the siege on Yemen was lifted.

Their ambitions, however, extend beyond Yemen.

The movement's frames its politics in opposition to US and Israeli power in the region.

Since 2023, the group has attacked more than 100 commercial ships in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, saying it was acting in solidarity with Palestinians during Israel's genocide in Gaza. The strikes were temporarily halted in May 2025 in a ceasefire deal with Washington, brokered by Oman.

In March, it began firing missiles at Israel in support of Tehran after the US and Israel launched their war on Iran.

How close are they to Iran?

Iran counts Ansar Allah as part of its "Axis of Resistance" alongside Hezbollah and Hamas, and has courted the group since at least the late 2000s. Much of the Houthi arsenal has been designed or supplied by Tehran.

The Houthis deny being an Iranian proxy. 

After the Riyadh strikes, Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said on Monday that Tehran was "deeply concerned" by the escalation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, and offered to help facilitate dialogue between the two sides.

How strong are they militarily?

The Houthi fighting force grew from an estimated 30,000 in 2015 to around 350,000 by 2024, although counts vary.

The group has no conventional navy and little air power, but it fields drones, explosive-laden drone boats and medium-range ballistic missiles that have reached targets about 2,000km away in Israel.

Why does the Bab al-Mandab matter?

The strait links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is the southern approach to the Suez Canal.

Its importance has grown since the war on Iran disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, driving up oil prices and leaving the Red Sea as a key alternative route for Saudi exports.

articles.title: 'Except Mecca and Medina': Chaos across Saudi airports as Houthis claim Riyadh strikes
articles.summary:
'Except Mecca and Medina': Chaos across Saudi airports as Houthis claim Riyadh strikes

Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 10/12/2026 - 10:38
Riyadh and Dammam airports were reported closed in a FlightRadar24 update, while Jeddah faced widespread cancellations and delays
A CCTV screengrab shows the moment King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was hit in a Houthi strike, 10 October 2026 (Saudi Media Ministry/AFP)
Off

Terminals across Saudi Arabia were left in chaos on Monday after repeated attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport and warnings issued by Yemen’s Houthi group. 

Several airlines halted operations and over a third of all planned flights in the country were cancelled.

Approximately 60 percent of flights set to depart from Riyadh on Monday were scheduled to be cancelled, while 99.7 percent of the airport’s flights were cancelled on Sunday, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium, cited by Reuters.

On Sunday, Flightradar24 reported that Riyadh and Dammam airports were closed.

Jeddah airport cancelled 156 flights, constituting 20 percent of all scheduled flights, while 374 flights, or 49 percent, were delayed. 

Saturday’s attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed 12 people and injured 309, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation. 

The death toll subsequently rose to 13 after an Indian national who had been injured in the strike died, according to Reuters.

A separate attack on Sunday killed a Pakistani resident and injured 11 others, according to the Saudi authorities.  

Airlines have also suspended services to the Saudi capital.

Reuters reported that Lufthansa cancelled flights to Riyadh until 16 October, while Air France-KLM extended its suspension through the end of October.

The US Federal Aviation Administration advised American airlines to exercise caution when operating in or over Saudi Arabia.

Houthi warning 

Yemen’s Houthi movement has warned airlines, shipping companies, airport employees and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, with the exception of airports serving Mecca and Medina.

In a statement posted on X on Sunday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group was renewing its warning to aviation and navigation companies, workers and travellers. 

Houthi forces warn against use of Saudi airports following Riyadh attack
Read More »

“The Yemeni armed forces renew their warning to all aviation and navigation companies, experts, staff, workers, and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace,” Saree said.

“The airports and airspace are exposed to targeting and constitute a theatre of operations for our forces, with the exception of the airports of Makkah and Madina,” he added. 

He urged people to “take our warnings seriously” and said Saudi Arabia would bear responsibility for failed interceptions.

The Houthis, officially called Ansar Allah, have claimed responsibility for the attacks on Riyadh airport, as well as additional strikes on Dammam airport and Saudi Aramco facilities, according to Reuters.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the group in Yemen described the deadly Riyadh attack as a “full-fledged war crime”.

International reaction

Several other regional and international nations have condemned the attack, including Iraq, the UAE, Qatar, Germany, France and Britain, as well as European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen and United Nations General Secretary Antonio Guterres. 

Attacks by 'Iran’s proxies' pushing region into spiral of violence, says EU on Riyadh airport strike
Read More »

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called the attack “contemptible” and a “dangerous escalation”, saying it explains “one of the reasons why the UK is providing support to Saudi Arabia in the form of air defences but also air-to-air refuelling” in an interview with Sky News on Sunday.

When asked if the UK’s support for the kingdom could go further, Streeting told the BBC that “potentially” it could. 

The airport has faced repeated targeting from the Sanaa-based group, but this alleged attack would mark the most deadly escalation in their “tit-for-tat” strikes with the neighbouring Gulf state. 

Houthi-affiliated media reported on Friday that Saudi strikes on the airport in the capital city of Sanaa killed two people, a day after their attacks against Riyadh airport killed three. 

Sanaa is demanding that Saudi Arabia lift its land, air and sea blockade of Yemeni territory under Houthi control in what it describes as a "blockade for a blockade".

Saudi Arabia and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government have launched repeated strikes across Yemen, hitting civilian infrastructure, including airports, but this has not prevented the Yemeni group from being able to launch missiles and drones back at the kingdom.

Inside Saudi Arabia

articles.title: Israeli elections: Grotesque court spectacle sets a chilling precedent
articles.summary:
Israeli elections: Grotesque court spectacle sets a chilling precedent

Submitted by Orly Noy on Thu, 10/08/2026 - 20:05
Ruling to uphold the disqualification of Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh shows the true face of our 'democracy'
Sami Abu Shehadeh, pictured at centre, and other Arab politicians attend a hearing at the Supreme Court in Jerusalem, on 1 October 2026 (Ilia Yefimovich/AFP)
Off

If Israel still had any masks left to conceal the depths of its anti-democratic descent, they were shattered in the Supreme Court last week, when an expanded panel of nine justices heard petitions seeking to disqualify all Arab lists from running for the Knesset, as well as two individual candidates: Hadash MK Ofer Cassif and Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh.

It is a ritual repeated in every Israeli election: the Central Elections Committee, a political body dominated by the governing coalition, broadly disqualifies Arab parties and individual candidates. The Supreme Court then overturns those decisions in order to preserve Israel’s image as a democratic state. 

This time, in a profoundly dangerous precedent, the court did not overturn the committee’s decision regarding Abu Shehadeh, and upheld his disqualification from running for parliament. 

This was not the only red line crossed. Under Israeli law, an individual or a list can be disqualified from running for the Knesset on several grounds, including rejecting Israel’s character as a Jewish and democratic state, and supporting armed struggle against the state. 

Because the first could theoretically be used not only to disqualify Arab parties, but also non-Zionist ultra-Orthodox parties, the court has over the years found ways around this obstacle.

As for supporting armed struggle, right-wing parties have long invested enormous resources in trying to pin this accusation on Arab parties and representatives. Every statement made by a Palestinian candidate over the years, every article they have written, every social-media post or event they have attended - all are examined under a magnifying glass, in hopes of somehow proving such support. 

This time, the “trophy” they found was an article by Abu Shehadeh published in Arabic on 8 October 2023, the day after the Hamas attack, offering an initial analysis of the event and the reality that had emerged.

Broad support

The petition to disqualify Abu Shehadeh on the basis of that article was filed by National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, the ideological descendant of Meir Kahane, whose own movement was declared a terrorist organisation and outlawed in 1994 after the Ibrahimi Mosque massacre, carried out by Kahanist Baruch Goldstein. 

The fact that the disqualification petition was filed by Ben Gvir - a man convicted of supporting a terrorist organisation, who had a framed photograph of the mass murderer Goldstein in his living room, and who celebrated his most recent birthday with a cake bearing a festive image of a noose, which has become his trademark - should alone have been enough for any decent party to reject it.

Yet this is where the first dangerous precedent emerged. Not only was the disqualification petition supported by the Jewish right and centrist opposition parties; it was also backed by the Democrats, led by Yair Golan - the party supposedly representing the Zionist left, which speaks frequently of “Jewish-Arab partnership”. 

Like everything else in the only democracy in the universe, even the right to be morally outraged is a privilege reserved exclusively for Jews

That partnership, it turns out, can easily be tossed into the garbage the moment the Zionist left seeks to prove its loyalty to the other Zionist parties with which it hopes to form the next government. For that purpose, they will not hesitate to throw under the bus a Palestinian leader engaged in a political struggle for justice and equality.

The second precedent set in this case is far more serious and dangerous. For the first time, the Supreme Court did not overturn an entirely political decision by the Central Elections Committee, and instead upheld Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification from running for the Knesset. 

This was despite the objections of a long list of prominent legal scholars, including former Deputy Attorney General Dina Zilber, law professor Barak Medina, academic David Harel, and even attorney Moshe Cohen-Eliya, a law professor associated with the far right, whose own analysis concluded that there was no legal basis for the disqualification. 

But these proceedings had very little, if anything, to do with law. More than anything, the case resembled a Shin Bet interrogation.

I sat in the courtroom, stunned, and watched this disgraceful hearing for more than three hours. The Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party was represented by Ben Gvir himself, and by attorney Ze’ev Wolf, previously convicted of murdering a Palestinian man in Jerusalem’s Old City in November 1992, two years after Rabbi Meir Kahane’s assassination. He was later pardoned.

This is the Jewish and democratic state: two men convicted of terrorism-related offences seeking to silence a Palestinian leader who has devoted his life to a political struggle for equality and justice. They are backed by the entire Zionist spectrum, from right to left, as well as by the Supreme Court itself.

Moral outrage

In a country whose political and military leaders have called for the indiscriminate annihilation of a civilian population and the starvation of more than two million people in Gaza; a country facing proceedings over the commission of genocide, and whose prime minister is the subject of an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court; in this country, a Palestinian public leader is given a show trial over an article he wrote.

This is Israeli democracy in all its glory.

There is not enough space here to recount all the miserable absurdities that unfolded during the hearing. But one thing in particular caught my attention: the emotionally charged vocabulary used by the justices and the lawyers on the right. One expression, above all, kept recurring: “disgust”.

Netanyahu won't stop until all Arab political parties are gone
Read More »

They felt disgust at the fairly elementary analysis in Abu Shehadeh’s article, in which he wrote that a pressure cooker eventually explodes, and that the struggle must be redirected towards political channels. They felt disgust at Cassif’s uncompromising solidarity with the oppressed. They felt disgust at Balad’s insistence on genuine equality and substantive democracy for everyone. 

Even I, a candidate ranked 15th on the Joint List for the Knesset, representing Balad, apparently managed to arouse a measure of their disgust because of an article in which I wrote about the obligation to distinguish between combatants and a civilian population.

The genocide in Gaza, with its tens of thousands of victims and two million people starved and dehydrated, many of whom have been orphaned, maimed and displaced, needless to say, did not arouse their disgust.

The Palestinians sitting in the courtroom, stone-faced as they watched this grotesque spectacle unfold, expressed no disgust.

Perhaps their souls, crushed day after day beneath the wheels of Jewish supremacy, are simply too exhausted to feel disgust anymore. Or perhaps they know all too well that, like everything else in the only democracy in the universe, even the right to be morally outraged is a privilege reserved exclusively for Jews.

The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Eye.
